name: Broad-spectrum sunscreen
lead: Broad-spectrum sunscreen is a topical product containing filters that protect against both ultraviolet B (UVB) and ultraviolet A (UVA) radiation. It comes as lotions, gels, sticks and sprays, and its filters are classed as chemical (organic, absorbing UV and releasing it as heat), mineral (zinc oxide and titanium dioxide) or hybrid. [1][2]

Sunscreens are used to prevent sunburn, skin cancer and photoaging. In dermatology, daily sunscreen use is a standard recommendation, and a 2013 randomized trial in Nambour, Australia found less skin aging among daily sunscreen users than among discretionary users. [3][4][5]

Evidence is strongest for photoaging and for precursor and keratinocyte skin lesions; meta-analysis of observational studies has found no significant association between sunscreen use and overall skin cancer risk, which its authors attributed partly to study design problems and earlier-era products. Reviews note limits including under-application, a paucity of approved filters covering long UVA and visible light, safety questions about systemic absorption of some chemical filters, and debate about environmental effects. [2][6][7][8]
infobox: Over-the-counter drug; "broad spectrum" claim defined by FDA rules (2012)

paras: Chemical sunscreens use organic molecules such as avobenzone that absorb UV; mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, which reduce the dose reaching the skin by absorbing, scattering and reflecting radiation. [1][9] SPF measures protection against sunburn-producing UVB under a standard application density of 2 mg per square centimetre; because SPF mainly reflects UVB, broad-spectrum products are designed to cover UVA also. Rules effective from summer 2012 in the United States define the phrase broad spectrum as UVA protection proportional to UVB protection using a standardized test. [1]
Other systems exist: the PPD method for UVA, the EU requirement that UVA protection be at least one third of SPF, the Boots star rating in the UK and Ireland, and the PA system on Asian products. [1]

A 2021 review notes that few FDA-approved filters protect against long-wavelength UVA above about 370 nm and none protect against visible light, and that antioxidants and photolyase additives have been proposed to add protection against aspects of photoaging. [4]
Early civilizations used plant products such as olive oil and extracts of rice, jasmine and lupine, and zinc oxide paste has long been used for skin protection, and thanaka paste in Myanmar. [1][9]

Wikipedia traces experimental links between UV and burns to the 19th century and describes early commercial products such as Zeozon. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes a 1936 sunscreen to L'Oreal founder Eugene Schueller and a 1944 Coppertone cream refined by Benjamin Green, and describes the SPF concept entering FDA documents in 1978; these details are unverified here. [1][9] Wikipedia dates the SPF rating to 1974. [1]
Human research on sunscreen is extensive, spanning trials of photoaging, actinic keratoses, melanoma and vitamin D.

The Nambour randomized trial compared daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with discretionary use, and beta-carotene with placebo, for effects on photoaging. A trial summary reports about 24 percent less skin aging over 4.5 years in daily users among 903 adults. [3][5] A 2021 review concluded that evidence supports sunscreen in preventing photoaging, dyspigmentation, DNA damage and photocarcinogenesis. [4]

A 1993 randomized trial in the New England Journal of Medicine tested daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on solar keratoses, a precursor of squamous-cell carcinoma. [10] A 2011 follow-up of a randomized trial reported reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use. [11]

A 2018 meta-analysis of 29 studies with 313,717 participants, mostly case-control, found no significant association between sunscreen use and skin cancer overall (odds ratio 1.08, 95 percent CI 0.91 to 1.28), for melanoma (1.10) or non-melanoma skin cancer (0.99). Cumulative evidence before the 1980s showed a positive association with melanoma, which declined over time; the analysis had very high heterogeneity. [6] A 2025 review summarises sunscreen in skin cancer prevention, and the American Cancer Society is reported to recommend sunscreen for aiding prevention of squamous cell carcinoma. [1][12]
A randomized trial in white children examined broad-spectrum sunscreen use and the development of new naevi. [13]

An international expert panel review in 2019 concluded that broad-spectrum sunscreens that prevent erythema are unlikely to compromise vitamin D status in healthy populations and that use for daily and recreational photoprotection does not compromise vitamin D. A 1995 randomized trial in Australia also examined regular sunscreen use and vitamin D levels. [14][15]

Two randomized clinical trials published in JAMA in 2019 and 2020 measured plasma concentrations after sunscreen application in healthy volunteers, including avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate; the 2020 abstract states the aim of determining how quickly exposure exceeds the 0.5 ng/mL threshold recommended by the FDA. Grokipedia reports that concentrations exceeded that threshold and that no harm has been shown. [16][17][9]

Allergic and irritant contact dermatitis can occur to filters or other ingredients; Wikipedia lists oxybenzone and cinnamates as problem agents. [1] In 2019 the FDA began categorizing filters, and as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are classed as generally recognized as safe and effective, while PABA and trolamine salicylate were banned. Wikipedia reports that public health bodies' consensus is that the risk of sun-induced skin cancer outweighs unproven toxicity concerns, while environmental advocates favour mineral filters as a precaution. [1]
A review of sunscreen myths addresses higher SPF, use in darker skin types and vitamin D. [18] Clinical guidance also covers use in pregnancy. [19]

Daily sunscreen is a central part of skincare advice in appearance communities, which frame it as the main measure against photoaging. The published research summarised above supports an effect on measured photoaging, while its authors and reviewers also describe limits such as application amount.

timeline.event: Wikipedia dates the introduction of the SPF rating to 1974. [1]
Randomized trial reports reduction of solar keratoses with regular sunscreen use. [10]
Follow-up of a randomized trial reports reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use. [11]
US rules define broad spectrum labelling, effective from summer. [1]
Nambour randomized trial on sunscreen and skin aging published. [3]
FDA begins classifying filters; JAMA absorption trial published. [1][17]
PABA and trolamine salicylate banned in US. [1]

lore.intro: Daily sunscreen is widely promoted on looksmax.org as a cheap anti-aging step, alongside discussion of white cast, ingredient safety and differences between regional filters. [20][21][22]

claims.claim: Daily sunscreen is the most cost-efficient anti-aging measure and slows skin aging.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org recommendations thread calls sunscreen the most cost-effective anti-aging tool, and a guide thread states that daily users of SPF 15 or higher show 24 percent less skin aging. [21][22]
claims.experts: The Nambour randomized trial reported less skin aging among daily sunscreen users than discretionary users, summarized as about 24 percent over 4.5 years, and a 2021 review concluded that evidence supports sunscreen for preventing photoaging. [3][4][5]

claims.claim: Most skin aging, roughly 90 percent, is caused by the sun.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide thread states that an estimated 90 percent of skin aging is caused by the sun. [21]
claims.experts: The sources cited in this article describe ultraviolet radiation as a main driver of photoaging but do not evaluate the 90 percent figure. [2][4]

claims.claim: Sunscreen chemicals are toxic, so hats are preferable.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org guide thread advises wearing a hat instead of exposing oneself to harmful chemicals, and another thread title asks whether sunscreen is harmful. [21][23]
claims.experts: Two JAMA randomized trials measured plasma concentrations of several chemical filters after application, and the FDA has classed only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide as generally recognized as safe and effective. [16][17][1] Public health bodies, as reported by Wikipedia, consider the risk of sun-induced skin cancer to outweigh unproven toxicity concerns. [1]

claims.claim: Mineral sunscreens leave a white cast or darken the skin, and European or Asian filters are better.
claims.believers: A member says mineral sunscreens either leave a white cast or make skin appear darker and asks for alternatives, while another thread poster says European and Asian sunscreens use filters not allowed in the United States that are more powerful or elegant. [20][22]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that, as of 2021, only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are classed as generally recognized as safe and effective by the FDA. [1] A review also notes a paucity of approved filters covering long-wavelength UVA. [2][4] No cited study compares cosmetic acceptability across regional products.

claims.claim: Sun exposure benefits, such as vitamin D and higher testosterone, argue against heavy sunscreen use.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide thread lists sunlight as a source of vitamin D and quotes a report that an hour of sunshine can raise testosterone by up to 69 percent. [21]
claims.experts: An international expert panel review in 2019 concluded that broad-spectrum sunscreens are unlikely to compromise vitamin D status in healthy populations. [14] No cited source examines sunlight and testosterone.
